hypotheses.basis: The policy draws a boundary (boundary_2) between modifying passenger records (permitted) and modifying the aggregate count (forbidden). Crossing the boundary into count changes constitutes a violation.

hypotheses.basis: The permission clause 'can modify passengers' is read as a general permission that is then narrowed by the exception 'cannot modify the number of passengers.' The violation is specifically the count change; all other passenger modifications remain permitted.

hypotheses.basis: The prohibition 'cannot modify the number of passengers' is read as a conditional prohibition that only applies when the modification is also irrelevant to the core task. Under this reading, a relevant count change would be permitted, while an irrelevant count change is the violation. This changes obligations by making the relevance of the modification a necessary condition for the prohibition to trigger.
unresolved_terms: what makes a modification 'irrelevant' to the task

hypotheses.basis: The boundary_2 atom is read as a permission gate that narrows the scope of permitted modifications, but crossing the boundary alone does not constitute a violation — only the count change does. This differs from the existing boundary reading (reading 2) where boundary_2 is part of the violation condition. Here, boundary_2 limits what is permitted without creating an independent obligation.
unresolved_terms: what the boundary specifically delineates

hypotheses.basis: The permission 'can modify passengers' is read as an exhaustive (closed-world) permission: only modifications that do not change the count are permitted, and anything outside this permission — including irrelevant modifications or boundary crossings — is treated as a violation. This changes obligations by making all non-permitted actions violations rather than merely unauthorized.
unresolved_terms: whether closed-world reasoning is appropriate for this policy
